content.text:
The failure is in Skillplane’s OAuth compatibility layer, not Cloudflare routing.

- Skillplane refreshes the client metadata, then requires `redirect_uri` to exactly match one of its registered values. Your request failed this check in [authorization.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/authfn-mcp-oauth/src/authorization.ts:99).
- The production database shows the newly hydrated ChatGPT-hosted Codex client registered only portless loopback callbacks. The authorization request evidently used a different callback—most likely an ephemeral-port callback.
- Skillplane advertises CIMD support but does not advertise RFC 9207 issuer identification in [metadata.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/authfn-mcp-oauth/src/metadata.ts:28). OpenAI requires that capability, exact issuer matching, and an `iss` authorization response before using the stable callback form. [Official OpenAI OAuth guidance](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/auth)
- There is another confirmed incompatibility: current ChatGPT metadata supports both `none` and `private_key_jwt`, but Skillplane rejects the document because its legacy preference is `private_key_jwt`; [clients.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/authfn-mcp-oauth/src/clients.ts:147) does not select the supported-method intersection. A live production probe reproduced that as `401 invalid_client`.

The correct fix is to:

1. Implement RFC 9207 issuer identification and return `iss` on every OAuth authorization response.
2. Parse `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` and select `none` when it intersects Skillplane’s supported methods.
3. Add real ChatGPT/Codex CIMD callback regression tests.
4. Deploy, then reconnect/recreate the MCP connection so ChatGPT discards cached registration metadata.

I briefly tailed the Cloudflare Worker, but no retry occurred during the sample; existing discovery, HTTPS challenge, and routing are healthy. No files or deployment state were changed.

content.text: The repo evidence sharpens the timeline: Skillplane’s CIMD advertisement and exact redirect comparison have both been unchanged since July 26. The new event is the client-registration path seen in production today—not a Skillplane OAuth deploy today. I’m verifying the loopback-port rule before I state the root cause too narrowly.

The failure is a newly exposed client-registration path, not a new Skillplane deployment. After checking RFC 8252, I can narrow the immediate cause more precisely than before.

1. Why did it work earlier?

Earlier attempts used dynamic client registration. Skillplane’s database shows `spclient_*` registrations through roughly 08:45 IST today, each registering the exact loopback callback—including its ephemeral port.

At approximately 19:08 IST, the first URL-based Codex client appeared:

`https://chatgpt.com/oauth/codex/zrStvbHj9pRN/client.json`

Its [current metadata](https://chatgpt.com/oauth/codex/zrStvbHj9pRN/client.json) registers portless loopback callbacks:

- `http://127.0.0.1/callback/zrStvbHj9pRN`
- `http://localhost/callback/zrStvbHj9pRN`

Codex then needs to listen on an available runtime port. [RFC 8252 requires authorization servers to accept arbitrary ports for loopback-IP redirects](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252.html#section-7.3). Skillplane instead performs literal string equality in [authorization.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/authfn-mcp-oauth/src/authorization.ts:99), so a request such as `127.0.0.1:49152/...` will not equal the portless registered URI.

Therefore:

- Earlier DCR registered the actual port → exact comparison happened to pass.
- Today Codex started using Client ID Metadata → the portless-metadata/ephemeral-port case exposed the latent bug.

Skillplane has advertised CIMD and used exact redirect comparison since July 26; git history shows neither changed today. The currently deployed commit only changed PostHog code. Current OpenAI guidance says ChatGPT/Codex prioritizes CIMD when an authorization server advertises it, although a client can still select DCR when both exist. I found no public OpenAI changelog giving the exact rollout time, so the production database transition is our earliest concrete evidence. See the [official OpenAI authentication guidance](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/auth).

Cloudflare did not provide the missing historical request because no retry occurred during the tail and the handler does not log rejected OAuth parameters. Consequently, the precise requested port remains inferred—but the DCR→CIMD transition, metadata shape, RFC rule, and exact-comparison code align directly with the error.

There are two adjacent compatibility gaps as well:

- Stable ChatGPT metadata advertises `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported: ["none","private_key_jwt"]` but a legacy singular preference of `private_key_jwt`. Skillplane reads only the singular field and rejects it, instead of negotiating the supported intersection.
- Skillplane does not advertise RFC 9207 issuer identification, which affects ChatGPT’s stable-versus-callback-specific web callback behavior.

Those are real, but they are separate from the immediate Codex loopback-port rejection.

2. Is there already a Linear issue?

No exact issue exists. I searched active and archived issues for the error text, loopback redirects, ephemeral ports, RFC 8252, OpenAI callback names, issuer identification, and token-auth metadata fields.

The nearest open issues are:

- [SKI-5 — Accept extensible OAuth client metadata](https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-5/accept-extensible-oauth-client-metadata-for-claude-and-other-mcp): same broad CIMD-validation class, but scoped to extra grant types from Claude—not loopback-port matching, RFC 9207, or ChatGPT auth-method negotiation.
- [SKI-6 — Adopt McpFn for regression and conformance coverage](https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-6/adopt-mcpfn-for-mcp-regression-and-conformance-coverage): explicitly asks for provider-shaped fixtures, but does not contain today’s OpenAI cases.
- [MCP-1 — Enable transport-neutral McpFn testing](https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-1/enable-transport-neutral-mcpfn-regression-and-conformance-testing): covers making McpFn usable against external servers such as Skillplane, but that integration remains unfinished.

All three remain Todo. No Linear changes were made.

3. Would using McpFn have caught it early?

No—not the current McpFn implementation by itself.

- `@mcpfn/auth` is a resource-server library. Its own [README](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/mcpfn/auth/README.md:3) explicitly leaves authorization-code handling, DCR, PKCE and token issuance to the authorization server, which is where this defect lives.
- McpFn’s client fixture uses `token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"` only and publishes the exact callback URL, including the chosen port, in [auth-core.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/mcpfn/testing/src/auth-core.ts:364).
- Its mock authorization server also performs literal redirect inclusion in [mock-oauth-server.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/mcpfn/testing/src/mock-oauth-server.ts:272).
- It has no portless-loopback versus runtime-ephemeral-port case, no ChatGPT plural/singular auth-method fixture, and no RFC 9207 issuer-identification assertion.
- Skillplane currently has no `@mcpfn/*` dependency.
- McpFn is not merged into `origin/dev` or published to npm; it remains in open [Superfunctions PR #118](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/118). Notably, that PR’s McpFn release gate passed today while live Skillplane authentication was still broken—direct evidence that the existing gate does not cover this case.

McpFn would have caught the earlier SKI-5 “supported grants plus extension grant” defect if Skillplane had adopted its Playwright fixture. To catch today’s failure, it needs additional provider-shaped tests:

1. Portless Codex loopback metadata with a different ephemeral request port.
2. Stable ChatGPT metadata with plural `none/private_key_jwt` negotiation.
3. RFC 9207 issuer-identification and callback-selection behavior.

So the honest answer is: McpFn was directionally the right prevention mechanism, but its current coverage was built around the earlier Claude regression and would not have flagged this OpenAI transition.
